caption:
Bleach (2001): the battle manga that dressed like a fashion magazine.

Tite Kubo could put five characters in the same white shirt and make every one of them read differently. Open collars. Loose ties. Rolled sleeves. One bare foot taking over the frame. Nothing here feels added after the character. The clothes are the character.

That is why the color pages can move from heavy winter layers to tartan tailoring, oversized hats, denim, fur, headphones, chocolate hearts and an all-white summer deck without losing anyone. Ichigo stays restless. Uryu stays precise. Renji makes everything louder. Rukia keeps it sharp. Orihime turns a sun hat into a whole scene.

Most shonen uses clothing to tell you where someone belongs. Bleach uses it to tell you how they want to be seen. The Soul Reapers spend the story in black, so every break into color becomes Kubo's private runway.

It didn't invent fashion in manga. It made style feel like part of the power system.

Seventy-four volumes. Fifteen years. Still more drip than most series ever manage.

Bleach, 2001–2016 — Tite Kubo
